title: Assessment of Lung Health Status by Analyzing Cough Sound Using Swaasa Artificial Intelligence Technology
abstract: Introduction: The crucial function of the respiratory system is the facilitation of blood gas exchange process. Spirometry is the diagnostic tool to detect and differentiate obstructive and restrictive respiratory diseases that impair this vital function. The need for a clinical setup, technical expertise, and patient compliance are certain limitations for utilizing spirometry in remote areas. Swaasa ® artificial intelligence (AI) platform, which has a Class B manufacturing license from India’s Central Drugs Standard Control Organization, is a validated “software as a medical device,” which aids in screening and diagnosis of respiratory diseases, unbounded by location, equipment and technical expertise. Objectives: The objectives of the study were to determine the “lung health index” and the “pattern of lung health” conditions among nursing students. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted utilizing the Swaasa ® AI platform among students of a nursing college in Central Karnataka in June 2023. Based on audiometric analysis of cough sounds, parameters such as underlying respiratory condition, cough count values, and respiratory symptoms experienced, ‘Swaasa’ AI platform derives pattern of respiratory condition (normal/obstructive/restrictive/mixed), ‘Lung Health Index,’ and presence or absence of lung health risk. Data collected in the Swaasa app were downloaded and analyzed using SPSS.v. 20. Results: Lung health risk was present in 58.2% of participants. Abnormal lung pattern was noted in 21.3% of participants (obstructive: 14.8%, restrictive: 2.5%, and mixed pattern: 4.1%). Conclusion: The Swaasa AI platform was utilized in this study to self-test lung health in real time without the need for a clinical setting. A high lung health index was found among 18% of participants. Studies adopting such cough sound analysis involving a larger population from wider geographic areas have to be conducted to detect and monitor respiratory diseases to increase its usage among the medical community in everyday clinical practice and also in remote areas.

title: Integrating Ai and Data Engineering In Iot Ecosystems: Streaming Data Management for Smart Devices
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies of the 21st century, revolutionizing how industries operate and how devices interact within interconnected ecosystems. IoT enables billions of smart devices to collect, process, and share data, fostering unprecedented innovation across sectors like healthcare, manufacturing, smart cities, and transportation. However, the rapid expansion of IoT ecosystems has given rise to significant challenges in managing the vast volume, velocity, and variety of data generated by these devices. Traditional approaches to data management and processing often fall short, particularly in environments requiring real-time responsiveness, seamless scalability, and reliable decision-making.Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) with advanced data engineering techniques offers a powerful solution to these challenges. AI brings capabilities such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and intelligent decision-making, which, when combined with robust data engineering practices, enable efficient streaming data management. This integration supports real-time data processing, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, and dynamic resource optimization, which are essential for creating intelligent IoT systems. By leveraging tools like real-time data pipelines, edge computing, and distributed architectures, AI-driven data engineering frameworks address critical issues, including data latency, resource constraints, and system scalability.This article delves into the intricate relationship between AI and data engineering within IoT ecosystems, focusing on streaming data management for smart devices. It explores the technical and theoretical underpinnings of integrating these fields, providing a comprehensive framework for optimizing IoT data streams. Key methodologies include employing machine learning algorithms to analyze real-time data, using edge computing to preprocess data closer to its source, and implementing scalable data pipelines for continuous processing.The findings of this study underscore the transformative potential of combining AI and data engineering in IoT ecosystems. Through experimental simulations and case studies, the research demonstrates how this integration enhances data flow efficiency, reduces latency, and improves the overall performance of IoT systems. For instance, in healthcare, AI-powered IoT devices enable real-time patient monitoring and predictive analytics, leading to improved medical outcomes. Similarly, in smart cities, integrated systems streamline traffic management, reduce energy consumption, and enhance public safety.This integration represents a paradigm shift in IoT ecosystems, laying the groundwork for intelligent, adaptive systems capable of meeting the demands of rapidly evolving industries. The study not only highlights the technological advancements enabled by this synergy but also identifies challenges such as integration complexity, resource limitations on edge devices, and the need for enhanced data privacy measures. Ultimately, this article serves as a blueprint for researchers, practitioners, and industry stakeholders aiming to unlock the full potential of IoT by bridging the gap between AI and data engineering.

title: PCAST Ignites Debate Among Hearing Health Professionals
abstract: Figure.: Roy Scott/Illustration SourceThe long-awaited report from the President's Council of Science and Technology Advisers (PCAST) has been met with widely differing reactions within the hearing health community. The report, which focuses on the 30 million Americans over 60 who have mild to moderate hearing loss, notes that no more than 30 percent of these individuals seek treatment. To improve these numbers, the PCAST report calls for addressing a number of factors, particularly the high cost of hearing aid technologies, barriers to access for hearing aids, and low levels of innovation in the field. A MIXED RECEPTIONFigure.: Lise HamlinThe number-one call that HLAA receives is about the affordability of hearing aids, said Lise Hamlin, HLAA's director of public policy. “We believe the PSAP recommendation is a good one. People on fixed incomes who age into hearing loss simply cannot afford to spend nearly $3,000 on one hearing aid. I don't have a lot of options to give them. People with more complex hearing loss—like me; I have a cochlear implant on one side and bilateral but not symmetrical hearing loss—will always need an audiologist. But for many other people, we think it would be beneficial to be able to get a basic device that allows them to enter the market at an affordable rate.” The PCAST report was far too narrow in its focus, addressing devices only rather than the full range of hearing health care, according to the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA).Figure.: Neil DiSarno, PhD“The report is all about getting people connected to devices, rather than looking at comprehensive services to the patient,” said Neil DiSarno, PhD, CCC-A, ASHA's chief staff officer for audiology. “It also leaves out the audiologist completely. It seems that they tried to produce an easy solution to a very complex problem.” ASHA opposes PCAST's first two recommendations, regarding a new OTC category of hearing aids and rescinding the FDA's PSAP guidance. If the FDA does move forward with “basic hearing aids” as a new category, however, ASHA calls for them to be sold with an open platform that would allow audiologists to view and adjust the parameters, rather than with the proprietary software most currently used. The American Academy of Audiology (AAA), in its own letter to PCAST, also called for stringent labeling should an OTC category of “entry level” hearing aids be created, stressing the importance of ensuring that these devices are not used for children because of the potential for long-term hearing damage.Figure.: Kim Cavitt, AuDIn contrast, the Academy of Doctors of Audiology (ADA) expressed its support for the PCAST recommendations—including 1 and 2—but with detailed qualifications. OTC hearing devices, ADA President Kim Cavitt, AuD, urged in a letter to the Council, should be specifically labeled, including a strong recommendation that a patient seek a comprehensive audiologic evaluation from an audiologist or physician prior to purchase—especially if the patient exhibits any of the warning signs of ear disease. Dr. Cavitt also noted the Academy's strong opposition to online self-diagnosis tools. “An individual needs a comprehensive hearing evaluation, complete with an otoscopic evaluation, air and bone conduction testing, speech testing in both quiet and noise, and a comprehensive case history to determine (1) the onset of the hearing loss, (2) the degree of hearing loss, (3) the type of hearing loss and (4) the etiology of the hearing loss,”she wrote. ‘CONSUMER ELECTRONICS’?Figure.: Ian Windmill, PhDMany hearing health professionals took exception to PCAST's classification of hearing aids in the same category as smartphones and other consumer electronics. “Audiologists and hearing aid dispensers have always operated under the framework that hearing aids are medical devices, as specified by the FDA. But PCAST characterizes them as consumer electronics, suggesting that their prices should have come down in the same way that other consumer devices have. These two concepts are disconnected,” said AAA President-Elect Ian Windmill, PhD. He also criticized the report's suggestion that OTC retail and online hearing tests can be sufficient for hearing evaluation and consumer self-diagnosis. “My FitBit can tell me my heart rate too. Does that mean it can diagnose treatable cardiovascular problems?” Categorizing OTC hearing aids and PSAPs as “consumer electronics” also eliminates any effective means of evaluating the quality of these devices, Dr. DiSarno noted. “We know there are devices out there that produce sound pressure levels that would certainly damage individuals’ hearing. There must be better oversight over these products, but industry standards for consumer electronics are quite lax relative to an agency like the FDA. While audiologists probably could and would recommend PSAPs to some of their patients, they need some way to be assured of the quality of the individual device, and right now there is no way of doing that.”Figure.: Andy BoppEncouraging self-diagnosis, self-treatment, and self-monitoring for mild to moderate hearing loss poses additional health risks to the consumer, said Andy Bopp, executive director of the Hearing Industries Association. “We found that 4 to 5 percent of 250,000 people who visited national hearing aid retail chains required referral to a doctor for red flags. Tumors are rare, but what if hearing problems are a symptom of another neurological issue, or an issue that is easily resolved, like wax removal?” He also noted that the rapid expansion of disruptive hearing aid distribution systems, including big box stores—which now account for about 10 percent of the hearing aid market—and the growth of online distribution systems that require a person to see a hearing professional have increased accessibility and affordability without sacrificing the key component of professional fittings. “Consumer Reports indicates that consumers can expect to pay from $500 to $3,000 for a hearing aid, which includes professional services,” Mr. Bopp said. Most hearing health organizations also expressed concern that the PCAST committee, which included experts in computers, technology, and aging but no one with specific expertise in hearing, such as an audiologist or ENT physician, made several off-base assumptions about the cost of hearing health care and how to address barriers to access. Japan's hearing aid market is fully deregulated in much the same way that the U.S. market would be if PCAST's recommendations were adopted. “If you have more profound hearing loss in Japan, some insurance coverage is available, but for others, there is no coverage. Over-the-counter hearing aids are readily available. You can buy hearing aids without a hearing exam at a wide array of retail locations such as jewelry stores and electronic stores. However, the hearing aid adoption rate is only 14 percent, and, more telling, the hearing aid satisfaction rate is only 36 percent,” Mr. Bopp said. “This compares to a 30 percent adoption rate and 81 percent satisfaction rates in the United States. If the FDA were to deregulate the hearing device market and to permit any manufacturer to make unfettered claims regarding any product, it is inevitable that unsubstantiated claims would mushroom, and the market would descend to the lowest common denominator. People lured to purchase substandard devices would inevitably be disappointed, and many would likely skip further treatment altogether.” SOME ISSUES UNADDRESSED With its primary focus on devices, the PCAST report also fails to address the role of professional diagnosis, evaluation and management in the cost of hearing aids, said Dr. Windmill. The report contrasts the average price of a hearing aid in 2014—$2,463—with the Department of Veteran's Affairs purchasing power of $400 per device, suggesting that there's a 600 percent markup in the private sector. “There's a mismatch there. All the costs of providing the device—diagnosis, selection, counseling, fitting, and follow-up—are bundled into the price in the private sector, whereas in the VA, that's subsidized by the federal government.” Although not fully supportive of the PCAST committee's conclusions, Dr. Windmill seemed resigned to the fact that the consumer perspective will continue to drive much of the public conversation surrounding hearing care. “The PCAST report suggests that making OTC products—whether you call them hearing aids or PSAPs or assistive listening devices—available without the aid of a professional would be good for the consumer, and it's what the consumer seems to want,” he said. “In many areas of health, if you have a minor concern—a sore shoulder, say—you can try something self-directed like aspirin or ice, and engage a professional only when the problem gets worse, or what you're doing doesn't work. The concept of self-directed care doesn't exist in hearing care. Either you live with it or you get a hearing aid. Consumers want some greater level of control over the decision of when to engage a professional, and some level of self-directed care.” The PCAST document will soon be followed by a much more comprehensive report from the Institute of Medicine's Committee on Accessible and Affordable Hearing Health Care for Adults. Due out this summer, the IOM report will be based on a series of public meetings held over the past year, which have addressed a wide array of issues ranging from best practices in hearing health care, bundling versus unbundling, coding and reimbursement, tele-audiology, the need for better hearing screening tools, new innovations in hearing aids and self-driven hearing solutions, and the development of a truly open wireless platform. POINTS OF CONTENTION OF PCAST REPORT The report from the President's Council of Science and Technology Advisers (PCAST) has sparked some controversy among hearing health community. title: Management of Hepatitis C in Children and Adolescents: An Update
abstract: EPIDEMIOLOGY An estimated 58 million people live with hepatitis C virus (PLWHCV) worldwide, of whom 3.2 million are children and adolescents.1 Approximately 1.5 million new infections occur annually, with 290,000 deaths attributed to HCV, the majority of which are cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. HCV prevalence varies by region, with viremia prevalence highest in eastern Europe (Ukraine 3.1%, Russia 2.9%, Moldova and Romania 2.5%), Africa (Gabon 5.9%, Burundi 3.6% and Egypt 2.1%), the Middle East (Syria 2.1%) and central Asia (Georgia 3.1%, Uzbekistan 3.1%, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan 2.7%).2 Rates of HCV in children correlate to the geographical prevalence in adults, with a recent meta-analysis estimating a global prevalence of 0.904% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.543–1.355).3 Directly-acting antivirals (DAAs), now licensed from 3 years of age, achieve cure rates of >95% and are the basis for World Health Organization (WHO) 2030 targets for HCV elimination: diagnosing 90% of PLWHCV with 80% accessing treatment. However, less than one-quarter of high-income countries are on target to achieve these goals.4 Elimination of HCV in children is possible, but only with enhanced efforts toward achieving WHO targets in adults. TRANSMISSION Person-to-person transmission of HCV is through infected blood and occurs nosocomially through the reuse and/or inadequate sterilization of medical equipment and via unscreened blood products. Community transmission occurs in people who inject drugs (PWID) and less frequently through tattooing as well as through sexual activities that lead to exposure to blood.5 The primary route of transmission in younger children is mother to child, with transmission rates of 5% in HCV mono-infection rising to 10% in HIV/HCV co-infection. In low-income settings, nosocomial transmission adds to the pediatric burden, while in older adolescents, transmission occurs through injecting drug use. Twenty-five percent of global PWID are under 25 years of age, rising to 43% in Eastern Europe.6,7 In regions with access to DAAs, rates of HCV viremia have fallen significantly, although further efforts are required to reach vulnerable populations and prevent re-infections.8 VIROLOGY HCV is a positive-stranded RNA virus of the Flaviviridae family. The HCV genome encodes 3 structural proteins [core capsid (C), envelope glycoprotein subunits (E1, E2)] and 7 nonstructural proteins (NS). The latter are targets for DAAs, inhibiting NS3, NS4A, NS5A and NS5B, preventing viral replication. HCV has enormous replicative capacity and is highly error-prone due to the low corrective activity of RNA polymerases, resulting in multiple variants. Eight major variants (genotypes 1–8), with further subtypes, vary in prevalence, global distribution, infectivity, pathogenicity and response to treatment. Genotype (GT) 1 is most prevalent globally and within Australasia, Europe and the Americas, with GT3 in Asia and GT4 within Africa and the Middle East. Initial DAA regimens were genotype-specific; however, subsequent pan-genotypic regimens offer therapeutic options for settings where genotyping is unavailable. Such genetic diversity and the ability of HCV to rapidly mutate and escape protective immune responses have hampered the development of pan-genotypic HCV vaccines.9 While the primary target of HCV is hepatocytes, extrahepatic manifestations (EHM) result from chronic immune activation, immune exhaustion and the potential for lymphoid malignant transformation. NATURAL HISTORY Chronic HCV infection is usually asymptomatic in childhood, although rare cases of advanced fibrosis and hepatic failure have been reported. HIV/HCV and hepatitis B virus/HCV co-infection are associated with accelerated disease progression and an increased risk of malignant transformation.10 EHM-HCV occurs in two-thirds of adults and, although less well documented in children, includes thyroid disease (subclinical and overt hypothyroidism), membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, cryoglobulinemia, myopathy and opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome. Limited data suggest HCV impacts on health-related quality of life in children and their families, with increased caregiver stress, HCV-associated stigma and poorer overall health outcomes, including impaired psychosocial and cognitive functioning.11 Neurocognitive deficits appear to correlate with levels of plasma inflammatory cytokines.12 In adults, EHM-HCV improves following treatment, but the impact of DAAs on childhood EHM, including neurocognitive functioning, requires elucidation. Following perinatal transmission, retrospective cohort data suggested spontaneous viral clearance (SVC) in 20%–40% of children by 4 years of age, associated with genetic polymorphisms in interferon-λ genes.13 However, recent prospective data suggests higher rates of both perinatal transmission and SVC, the latter nearer to 66% (95% CI: 50.1–81.6), occurring at a median age of 12 months.14 DAAs are available from 3 years, and while earlier therapy would result in significant overtreatment, it would have advantages in regions with high rates of loss to follow-up postpartum and potentially modifying neurocognitive deficits related to chronic HCV infection. DIAGNOSIS Initial HCV screening is performed through HCV-antibody testing. However, a positive HCV-antibody test cannot discriminate between previous infection (treated or following SVC) and current viremia. A positive HCV-antibody test should be followed by quantitative or qualitative nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for the detection of HCV-RNA.2,15 A negative HCV-antibody test within 6 months of HCV exposure requires NAAT or repeat antibody testing at least 6 months postexposure.16 The recommendations for HCV screening differ for perinatally exposed young children, as maternal HCV antibodies may persist for the first 18 months of life. Only NAATs should be performed before the age of 18 months, with serological testing recommended from 18 months of age.17 To improve HCV diagnosis and linkage to care, particularly among marginalized groups, several strategies have been acknowledged by the latest WHO recommendations. These include HCV point-of-care viral load NAAT assays, HCV core antigen detection as an alternative approach to diagnose viraemia in settings where access to NAAT is limited, reflex RNA HCV testing in patients with a positive HCV antibody, use of dried blood spot specimens for serology and NAAT and HCV self-testing.15,17,18 SCREENING WHO recommends screening for people at increased risk of HCV infection: migrants from endemic regions, health-care workers, PWID, people in prisons and other closed settings, men who have sex with men, sex workers, people living with HIV or hepatitis B virus, and children born to mothers living with HCV viremia. In settings with intermediate or high HCV antibody seroprevalence in the general population (defined as >2% or >5%, respectively), all adults should have routine access to and be offered testing.17 In 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention additionally recommended HCV universal screening at least once for all adults ≥18 years old and during each pregnancy, except where HCV prevalence is <0.1%.19 Universal HCV screening is a crucial component of the HCV elimination strategy, and HCV testing in pregnancy is essential for an appropriate follow-up and early diagnosis and treatment of perinatally exposed children. TREATMENT The development of highly effective oral DAAs has transformed the management of pediatric HCV infection since their first approval for adolescents in 2017. Registration and real-world studies demonstrated high efficacy [sustained virological response (SVR) rates >95%] and safety of DAAs in children and adolescents. Table 1 summarizes the 6 regimens currently used in children and adolescents, with their activity, regulatory approvals, formulations, doses, and treatment duration. Administration; Y, years. The goal of anti-HCV treatment is to cure the infection and thereby avoid the progression of liver disease, to prevent onward viral transmission, to remove the stigma associated with HCV infection and to improve the quality of life of patients and their families. The endpoint of therapy with DAA is SVR defined as the absence of HCV-RNA 12 weeks after the end of treatment (SVR12). The recently updated recommendations of WHO, the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases/Infectious Diseases Society of America (AASLD/IDSA), the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL), and the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) recommend antiviral treatment for children and adolescents above 3 years of age, regardless of disease severity.15,20–22 Pangenotypic and genotype-specific DAA regimens are equally recommended; pangenotypic regimens can simplify access to treatment as they do not require prior assessment of genotype and/or baseline resistance-associated substitutions. First-line studies in children do not show significant variation by DAA regimen in safety, tolerability or efficacy with high SVR rates achieved independent of genotype. Regimens with the shortest duration are preferable to improve treatment compliance. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir is generally considered a second-line treatment for individuals who have failed a previous regimen. Although not approved by the European Medicines Agency and the United States Food and Drug Administration, the combination of sofosbuvir plus daclatasvir is recommended by the WHO as a pangenotypic pediatric DAA regimen.15 This combination is less expensive and easily available and could therefore expand global access to HCV treatment in settings with the highest burden in children. Data on antiviral treatment in children 3–5 years old are limited due to the low number of patients included in published studies.15 Overall, data show high efficacy and tolerability in this age group; however, difficulty in taking oral medication, even in granular formulation, can be a major limitation. Poor adherence and early treatment discontinuations due to nonvirological reasons were the main causes of treatment failure in the sofosbuvir/velpatasvir registration trial in children 3–5 years of age, with an SVR12 of 83%.23 As recommended by the recent ESPGHAN position paper, a swallowability assessment should be done before starting DAAs, with treatment deferred for those unable to swallow the locally available drug formulation.22 Similar issues may occur for older children with neurological comorbidities, such as autism spectrum disorder, although data on this particular group are currently missing.12 PREVENTION OF PERINATAL TRANSMISSION HCV screening for people of childbearing age or prepregnancy is the main strategy to prevent perinatal transmission, providing the opportunity to cure the infection with DAAs before a possible pregnancy. Universal screening during each pregnancy is, however, of paramount importance to link the pregnant person to hepatitis care, starting DAAs after the completion of breastfeeding, and for HCV screening in the child and previous offspring.24 Notably, in the case of a pregnant person with a positive HCV-antibody and a negative NAAT, the individual should be considered as not currently infected, that is, has undergone SVR or successful treatment. The infant does not require further investigation or follow-up unless there is an ongoing risk of maternal re-infection during the pregnancy19 Currently, there are no large-scale published data on the safety and efficacy of DAAs in pregnant people, and none are licensed for use in pregnancy. However, scattered data from small cohorts suggest a high SVR12 without significant adverse effects.25,26 Therefore, both EASL and AASLD/IDSA guidelines acknowledge that treatment can be considered during pregnancy, or continued in the case of accidental conception during treatment, on a case-by-case basis, with a multidisciplinary approach and after a discussion with the patient about the potential risks and benefits.20,21 Expanding the use of DAAs during pregnancy would be crucial to reduce the burden of perinatal transmission. The international registry Treatment in Pregnancy for Hepatitis C (TiP-HepC Registry) collects data on DAA treatment during pregnancy, aiming to document large-scale data on outcomes and support appropriate decision-making.27 The risk of perinatal HCV transmission is not reduced by cesarean section or by the avoidance of breastfeeding, with the latter only recommended in HCV/HIV co-infection for women in line with HIV prevention guidance. The optimal timing for HCV screening in perinatally exposed children is debated. The main issue with testing at 18 months of age is poor attendance, with rates achieved rarely above 50%.28 A large single-center study demonstrated that HCV-RNA testing of exposed infants 2–6 months old led to reliable diagnostic results that correlated with antibody testing at 18 months.29 Current evidence suggests that a single HCV-RNA test at 2–6 months may be most effective in both health outcomes and cost.30 PATIENT INVOLVEMENT The importance of the third-sector initiatives in supporting individuals both in HCV testing and subsequently through treatment cannot be overemphasized, particularly for vulnerable and marginalized populations such as PWID, those in prison and the homeless. Peer support also reduces stigma, enables status sharing and facilitates family-based screening, including children of women LWHCV. CONCLUSION Global efforts are underway to achieve the WHO goals for HCV elimination. Strategies include increasing HCV diagnoses, especially in high-risk and marginalized groups, and ensuring the linkage to care for newly diagnosed PLWHCV. Universal treatment with DAA in children >3 years of age is now recommended and is highly successful. DAA treatment during pregnancy, currently under investigation, holds the potential to significantly reduce perinatal transmission.

title: Leveraging Python for Predictive Maintenance in Medical Equipment
abstract: This comprehensive research paper explores the application of Python-based predictive maintenance techniques in the medical equipment industry. By harnessing Python's robust data analysis and machine learning capabilities, healthcare providers and medical device manufacturers can significantly enhance equipment reliability, reduce downtime, and improve patient care. This study examines the implementation of predictive maintenance models, data processing techniques, and integration with Internet of Things (IoT) systems to create a holistic solution for medical equipment maintenance. The paper also addresses cybersecurity considerations and presents case studies demonstrating the effectiveness of Python-based predictive maintenance in real-world healthcare settings.

title: AI-Based Predictive Maintenance in Medical Equipment
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Unplanned medical equipment failures disrupt clinical workflows, delay patient care, and impose substantial financialcosts -- a single MRI scanner failure during peak scheduling can cancel 12-18 patient examinations and cost USD15,000-30,000 in lost revenue and emergency repair charges. Predictive maintenance (PdM) leverages sensor data andmachine learning to forecast equipment failures before they occur, enabling proactive servicing that minimises downtimewhile avoiding the waste of excessive scheduled maintenance. This study presents the AI-Based Predictive Maintenancefor Medical Equipment Framework (AIPMEF), evaluating five PdM approaches -- threshold-based condition monitoring,statistical degradation modelling, supervised failure classification, deep learning anomaly detection, and digital twinsimulation -- across four equipment categories: diagnostic imaging systems (MRI, CT, X-ray), laboratory analysers,patient monitoring networks, and surgical robotic platforms. Our Predictive Maintenance Performance Score (PMPS)integrates failure prediction accuracy, lead time adequacy, false alarm rate, maintenance cost reduction, and clinicalworkflow preservation. Deep learning anomaly detection achieved the highest PMPS (0.918) through convolutionalautoencoders that learn normal operational signatures from 14.6 million sensor readings and detect deviation patterns8.4 days before failure onset, while digital twin simulation achieved the highest lead time (12.6 days) throughphysics-informed models that project component degradation trajectories from current operating conditions.

title: Fault diagnosis of large-scale medical equipment
abstract: Large-scale medical equipment is very important for comprehensive hospitals. Fault monitoring and diagnosing technologies for large-scale medical equipment have to been available to make full use of them. This paper introduces the evolution of equipment fault diagnosis. After comparing conventional technology and intelligent one, this paper lays emphasis on the latter.

title: Engineering AI-Driven Predictive Maintenance Systems for Medical Equipment
abstract: The standard of patient care has gotten a lot better as medical technology has grown so quickly. But the dependability and life of medical tools are very important for keeping these progresses going. Unplanned downtime because of broken equipment can make it harder to care for patients and cost more to maintain. Scheduled checks and fixes done after the fact are common ways of maintaining things the old way, which might not catch problems before they break. This paper shows a new way to use AI-driven systems for predicted repair on hospital tools. Using machine learning algorithms and IoT (Internet of Things) devices, the suggested system checks on the health of equipment all the time, looks at data in real time, and guesses when problems might happen before they do. The AI model is taught by looking at old data from medical devices to find trends of wear and failure. This lets repair plans be made ahead of time. This forecast method increases the usage of equipment, lowers the cost of upkeep, and makes sure that medical gadgets are working at their best, which makes healthcare centres more efficient overall. In addition, the method makes medical operations safer by lowering the chance that tools will break down at crucial times. Case studies from healthcare settings show how well the system works in different kinds of medical technology, like surgery tools, testing machines, and life-support systems. The paper talks about the problems with execution, like combining data and making sure the model is correct, and gives ways to get around these problems. In the end, the suggested AI-driven predictive maintenance system would completely change how medical equipment is handled, leading to better care for patients, lower costs, and flawless operations.

title: AI-Enabled Predictive Maintenance of Medical Equipment for Energy and Waste Reduction
abstract: Hospitals are energy- and waste-intensive systems. Inpatient buildings dominate the sector’s electricity and gas consumption, and healthcare waste streams—especially device-associated disposables—increase environmental burdens. AI-enabled predictive maintenance (PdM) offers a dual lever: (1) reducing energy use by keeping assets operating at efficient points, and (2) preventing avoidable waste by extending component life, reducing emergency spares, and avoiding device-induced clinical workflow disruptions. In this study, an end-to-end architecture is developed by integrating multi-modal sensing (electrical, thermal, acoustic, vibration), computerized maintenance management systems (CMMS), risk-based maintenance under International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)/International Organization for Standardization standards (ISO 60601, 62353/62304, 81001-5-1), and learning pipelines (self-supervised anomaly detection, remaining useful life estimators, and carbon-aware work order scheduling). Using representative hospital archetypes and equipment classes (imaging, patient monitoring, laboratory analyzers, sterilizers, and pumps), energy, downtime, and waste avoidance are simulated under baseline preventive maintenance (PM) versus PdM with alternate equipment management. Results showed that 10–22% site electricity reduction was achieved, attributable to equipment efficiency and optimized duty-cycling, 18–35% fewer unplanned failures, and a 12–28% reduction in associated consumable waste and emergency part scrappage across scenarios, while maintaining compliance with Joint Commission/Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and IEC safety testing intervals. We discuss cybersecurity (IEC 81001-5-1) and the trustworthiness of AI, present a governance model linking CMMS events to carbon telemetry, and provide an implementation roadmap.

title: Research on Medical Device Fault Diagnosis and Maintenance Optimization Based on Big Data
venue: Frontiers in artificial intelligence and applications
abstract: In order to solve the problems of inaccurate fault detection results, long detection time and high missed detection rate because the time-frequency characteristics of fault signals are not analyzed in the circuit fault detection of medical devices, the research on fault diagnosis and maintenance optimization of medical devices based on big data is put forward. In this paper, wavelet packet analysis is used to analyze the time-frequency characteristics of fault signals, and the fault signals are decomposed layer by layer to obtain the signal frequency band energy. The energy of each frequency band is set as the element of fault feature vector, and the fault signal features are extracted. The extracted features are used as training samples to train the BP neural network, and the test samples are used to test the BP network to obtain different circuit fault types, and finally the circuit fault detection of medical devices is realized. The experimental results show that the missed detection rate of the circuit fault of the medical electroencephalograph by the proposed method is less than 9%, which is obviously lower than the other two methods, indicating that the proposed method can obtain more accurate fault detection results. Conclusion: The missed detection rate of the circuit fault of medical electroencephalograph by the proposed method is less than 9%, which is obviously lower than the other two methods, indicating that the proposed method can obtain more accurate fault detection results.

title: Risk-Based Predictive Maintenance in Medical Device Manufacturing Using Azure Databricks and SAP HANA
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a risk-based predictive maintenance framework specifically tailored for medical device manufacturing operations within regulated healthcare environments. Utilizing Microsoft Azure Databricks for scalable machine learning and SAP HANA for real-time in-memory data processing, the solution analyzes IoT sensor data and maintenance logs to anticipate equipment failure. The framework adheres to FDA CFR Part 11 compliance, embedding features such as digital signatures, audit trails, and traceability. Results from a pilot implementation demonstrate a 28% reduction in unplanned downtime and 40% improvement in audit preparation efficiency. This white paper serves as a guide for technical professionals aiming to enhance predictive capabilities and regulatory readiness in smart healthcare manufacturing.

title: Generative Model-Based Predictive Maintenance Frameworks for Early Failure Detection in Safety-Critical Medical Devices
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Medical equipment functions in safety critical conditions where the sudden failure of the equipment may lead to serious clinical impacts such as patient injuries, missed treatment, and compliance with regulatory policies. Since medical devices are becoming more and more connected, software-based, and data-intensive, the most important concern has become to sustain their reliability. Conventional approaches to the maintenance of medical devices are mainly either reactive or schedule-based, responding to failures when they happen or fixed cycles. These types of method are not usually adequate in modeling fine-scale degradation trends and precursors of failure, especially in non-linear and high-dimensional operational data of modern medical devices.Predictive maintenance has been a promising paradigm of enhancing device reliability whereby early detection of failure and proactive action is made. Nevertheless, other available predictive maintenance systems are based on rule-of-thumb or discriminative machine learning models that need labeled failure data, which can be unavailable, incomplete, or expensive to acquire in medical practice. This paper will solve these shortcomings by suggesting a generative model-based predictive maintenance system to identify early failure in safety-critical medical machines. Generative models can also successfully detect deviations and patterns of degradation that can predict failures in normal operations by learning the underlying probability distribution of normal operation, even without the need to cover a large labeled set.The framework proposed combines the most recent generative modeling methods to harness the time-related dependencies, the multivariate relationship and changing performance aspects of medical devices. It is conducive to immediate early Sign of anomaly and the precedents of failure, in order to take the maintenance action early enough before the critical faults appear. The framework is so structured in such a way that it is versatile to a wide variety of medical devices and operational settings and is compatible with clinical operations and regulatory standards.The most significant contributions of the work are a single architecture of generative predictive maintenance that is specific to safety-critical medical devices, a methodical presentation of early warning through generative modeling, and an evaluation perspective focusing on the early warning performance, but not on post-failure performance. The results indicate how generative models can be used to greatly improve the safety of medical devices, reduce downtimes, and help maintain more resilient and proactive healthcare technology management.

title: Support Vector Machine - Based Predictive Maintenance with Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency for Critical Medical Equipment
abstract: This study presents an SVM based predictive maintenance framework enhanced by Term Frequency Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) feature extraction for critical medical equipment. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset from the Malaysian Ministry of Health's Asset and Services Information System (ASIS), comprising over 10,000 maintenance records refined to 3,582 validated entries, we address the challenge of unstructured textual data through advanced preprocessing and classification into seven distinct failure categories. TF-IDF vectorization transformed technician descriptions into high-dimensional feature spaces, substantially outperforming basic encoding methods. Comparative analysis of four machine learning models revealed SVM as the optimal classifier, achieving 94.70% accuracy with 61% improvement over baseline performance without semantic features. This research demonstrates the critical role of feature engineering in predictive maintenance systems and provides a scalable AI framework for enhancing equipment reliability in healthcare environments. The integration of semantic analysis with machine learning offers significant potential for real-world deployment in medical equipment monitoring systems.

title: Self-Testing Medical Devices for the Detection, Diagnosis or Management of Health Conditions A Public Health Perspective
abstract: Self-tests, also known as home –tests, are typically sold over the counter (OTC) in pharmacies and allow users to test self-collected specimens and interpret the results in the comfort of their homes without the need of a trained or licensed health professional. These tests differ from home-collection tests, which require mailing or taking the sample to a laboratory or clinic for processing analysis and interpretation. Self-testing technologies have proven their diagnostic capabilities, but also are a powerful tool for clinical prevention, avoiding complications of diseases like diabetes, and preventing spread of infectious diseases like HIV and COVID-19. The fact that these products can be bought in pharmacies creates a niche for the pharmacist to get involved in curtailing epidemics. This chapter presents the evolution and current use of self-tests in monitoring diabetes and in identifying new cases of HIV and COVID-19. It argues that self-testing for monitoring and diagnosis of diseases cannot be ignored as a prevention tool. As primary healthcare services adopt patient-centered care and shared clinical decision-making, the ability to empower patients with point of care tests is fundamental. Concurrently to the dissemination of the home self-testing technologies, there is a need to educate patients to use, understand, and manage the diagnostic results. To fully benefit from self-testing technology, there is a need for systemic approach linkage to care after the test is performed.

abstract: The aspect of predictive maintenance of Medical Internet of Things (MIoT) devices may be discussed as a significant enhancement of the healthcare technology management. The predictive maintenance concerning the integration of IoT sensors with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) will enable data to be obtained in real-time and predictive faults and data-driven decisions about necessary medical devices. This would save time, maintenance cost and enhance patient safety by making the device reliable at all times. The chapter explores the architecture, technologies, problems, and applications of predictive maintenance in healthcare settings with an emphasis on how this concept may be used to switch between reactive and proactive maintenance methods and support intelligent, efficient, and sustainable medical regimes in the digital age.

title: Feature Extraction, Risky Classifications and Fault Diagnosis on Rolling Bearings of EEG Signals Denoised using Stationary Wavelet Transform of Patient Monitoring and IoT

abstract: BACKGROUND: One of the primary causes of sleep disorders, depth of anesthesia, coma, encephalopathy's and brain death in the world is epilepsy. EEG is most often used to diagnose epilepsy which causes the abnormalities in EEG readings. Different high-resolution anatomical imaging techniques are used to detect these abnormalities like MRI, PET, CT, etc. Methods: SWT method will be an enhanced system from wavelet transform. It may be fit for the signal for time-invariant on the break down also enhance those force of indicator denoising. SWT additionally employs upsampled technique at every level of decay for those signs. The decay of SWT produces the coefficients from claiming close estimation and points in the same length. The DWT will be actualized by a channel bank that decomposes those indicators over progressive coarser approximations. The output of the low pass and high pass filter coefficients is decomposed to the next level and further proceeds up to N levels. The yield of the wavelet decay may be that close estimation and the point of interest coefficients which would get to each level of decay. This system consists of five main processing steps: acquisition, pre-processing, feature extraction, feature selection and classification. RESULTS: This paper overviews some of the current state-of-the-art IOT systems and presents the statistical-based algorithm used for each processing step. CONCLUSION: This paper also provides a comparison of the performance of the existing approaches.

title: Specifications of the modern information system for maintenance of medical equipment in healthcare
abstract: Effective management of the maintenance of medical equipment (ME), especially high-tech one, is one of the main issues for the quality of health care, for the provision of cost-effective health services and for saving , even in developed countries, insufficient resources. Medical equipment maintenance (EM) includes all activities related to ensuring an adequate level of service and limiting the downtime of medical equipment in a healthcare organization. Traditionally, EM is categorized as preventive maintenance (PM) and corrective maintenance (CM). The principle of PM is prediction. PM can be planned and predictive, ie. Just-In-Time (JIT) maintenance. Predictive maintenance can only be applied to new high-tech medical devices that have built-in self-testing. Planned preventive maintenance is carried out in accordance with the maintenance plan for a certain period of time. As a rule, when creating the plan, we follow the manufacturer's recommendations for preventive maintenance of ME given in the technical documentation of the ME, especially in the instructions for the maintenance of the ME. Predictive or JIT maintenance makes it possible to detect and solve the problem before problems and contingencies actually occur, and this is done on the basis of intelligent monitoring and analysis of the state of ME at the right moment, which ensures the optimal time for intervention, so that maintenance performed only when necessary. The information system for the management of the maintenance of ME in healthcare institutions would interconnect healthcare institutions and enable the fast and safe exchange of data and information related to the maintenance of ME and enable the optimal maintenance of ME in healthcare institutions, increasing the availability of this equipment, especially high-tech equipment, with significant reduction of the total cost of maintaining ME (of the order of 30%). One of the main reasons for the unsustainability of the existing approach to the maintenance of ME in the healthcare institutions of Serbia is that each healthcare institution independently takes care of the maintenance of its own ME. This approach is expensive and significantly affects high maintenance costs. This approach needs to change.

title: Factors determining patients' intentions to use point-of-care testing medical devices for self-monitoring: the case of international normalized ratio self-testing
venue: Dove Medical Press (Taylor and Francis Group)
abstract: Syed Ghulam Sarwar Shah,1 Julie Barnett,1 Jasna Kuljis,2 Kate Hone,2 Richard Kaczmarski31Multidisciplinary Assessment of Technology Centre for Healthcare, 2Department of Information Systems and Computing, Brunel University London, Uxbridge, Middlesex, UK; 3Department of Haematology, Hillingdon Hospital, Uxbridge, Middlesex, UKPurpose: To identify factors that determine patients' intentions to use point-of-care medical devices, ie, portable coagulometer devices for self-testing of the international normalized ratio (INR) required for ongoing monitoring of blood-coagulation intensity among patients on long-term oral anticoagulation therapy with vitamin K antagonists, eg, warfarin.Methods: A cross-sectional study that applied the technology-acceptance model through a self-completed questionnaire, which was administered to a convenience sample of 125 outpatients attending outpatient anticoagulation services at a district general hospital in London, UK. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, factor analyses, and structural equation modeling.Results: The participants were mainly male (64%) and aged ≥ 71 years (60%). All these patients were attending the hospital outpatient anticoagulation clinic for INR testing; only two patients were currently using INR self-testing, 84% of patients had no knowledge about INR self-testing using a portable coagulometer device, and 96% of patients were never offered the option of the INR self-testing. A significant structural equation model explaining 79% of the variance in patients’ intentions to use INR self-testing was observed. The significant predictors that directly affected patients' intention to use INR self-testing were the perception of technology (β = 0.92, P < 0.001), trust in doctor (β = −0.24, P = 0.028), and affordability (β = 0.15, P = 0.016). In addition, the perception of technology was significantly affected by trust in doctor (β = 0.43, P = 0.002), age (β = −0.32, P < 0.001), and affordability (β = 0.23, P = 0.013); thereby, the intention to use INR self-testing was indirectly affected by trust in doctor (β = 0.40), age (β = −0.29), and affordability (β = 0.21) via the perception of technology.Conclusion: Patients’ intentions to use portable coagulometers for INR self-testing are affected by patients' perceptions about the INR testing device, the cost of device, trust in doctors/clinicians, and the age of the patient, which need to be considered prior to any intervention involving INR self-testing by patients. Manufacturers should focus on increasing the affordability of INR testing devices for patients’ self-testing and on the potential role of medical practitioners in supporting use of these medical devices as patients move from hospital to home testing.Keywords: oral anticoagulation, INR self-testing, technology-acceptance model, trust in doctor, home testing, affordability, structural equation modeling

title: Predictive Maintenance of Equipment Driven by Machine Learning
abstract: Industry is the leading sector of the national economy, and equipment maintenance, as a key link within it, ensures the stability of industrial production, improves production efficiency, and is crucial to industrial development. This paper studies the current application status and future development of machine learning-based equipment predictive maintenance in mechanical manufacturing through literature review and case analysis. The research reveals that machine learning algorithms, such as supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and deep learning, can significantly enhance the accuracy of predictive maintenance. Case studies on medical equipment using Weibull Distribution, new energy vehicles using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and concrete-filled steel tubular shear walls using Random Forest demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms in predicting failures and optimizing maintenance strategies. The findings suggest that integrating machine learning with predictive maintenance can reduce costs, improve efficiency, and enhance safety. Future work should focus on multi-technology integration and industry-specific customization to further advance the field.

title: Fault diagnosis and maintenance optimization for interconnected systems
abstract: For many systems, like medical devices, nuclear reactors, and transportation systems, an adequate maintenance optimization approach is essential to ensure high levels of reliability and safety while keeping operational costs low. A promising approach towards this goal is condition-based maintenance, which plans maintenance only when the system health indicates a need for it. To infer the system health, monitoring devices are installed to collect health-related data. The path from the monitoring data to a maintenance schedule then involves the following steps: 1. fault diagnosis, i.e. detecting abnormal system behavior and identifying its cause; 2. failure prognosis, i.e. predicting future system health; 3. maintenance optimization, i.e. determining the required type of maintenance as well as the optimal time to perform the maintenance task. Although various methods have been published for all three tasks, discrepancies still exist between the assumptions made in the literature and the conditions encountered in practice. These discrepancies include, e.g., unrealistic assumptions regarding the absence of component interdependencies and regarding the (number of) available monitoring signals. This thesis contributes to resolving these discrepancies by proposing methods for fault diagnosis, failure prognosis, and maintenance optimization, particularly focusing on narrowing the gap between theory and practice. When treating the individual tasks, the dependencies between fault diagnosis, failure prognosis, and maintenance optimization are explicitly taken into account.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Medical Device Maintenance
abstract: The increasing complexity and criticality of medical equipment in modern healthcare systems demand reliable and intelligent maintenance strategies to minimize downtime and ensure patient safety. In traditional predictive maintenance, it typically relies on data aggregation in a centralized manner, which poses data privacy and security concerns. In view of those risks associated with traditional data aggregation, a privacy-preserving FL approach for predictive maintenance in the healthcare setting is proposed in this work. This allows different healthcare institutions to collaborate for a common goal and learn together through model aggregation in a manner that no institution shares its operational or sensor data. In fact, each healthcare institution can develop its own DL-based model using its own MD’s TS data. However, the updated model data can pose SII, which can be protected using DP. At the central server, the aggregation strategy FL’s natural requirement of dealing with different data distributions can be handled with FedProx aggregation. The experimental performance indicates that the proposed framework provides performance comparable to that of the C-H model while performing much better than the L-H model and preserving data confidentiality. This further supports that data confidentiality can be maintained through FL. Finally, in this paper, it has been shown that the feasibility and potential of privacy-preserving FL can be applied in MD’s preventive maintenance.

title: Deep Learning-Based Fault Diagnosis for CAN Bus
abstract: The Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, as a widely adopted communication protocol in real-time control systems, has played a crucial role in automotive electronic control systems, industrial automation systems, and even medical devices, owing to its outstanding real-time performance, high reliability, and excellent multi-node data exchange capabilities. However, in the event of a fault occurring in any node on the CAN bus, all interconnected devices on the bus may potentially be affected. Therefore, effective fault diagnosis for the CAN bus is of significant importance. Addressing this challenge, this paper proposes a technical solution that combines One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1DCNN) and Long Short-Term Memory Network (LSTM). The proposed 1DCNN-LSTM model achieves precise fault diagnosis by real-time monitoring of voltage changes in the CAN bus. Experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, showing a higher fault diagnosis accuracy compared to traditional methods relying solely on 1DCNN.

title: The design of classifiers for condition monitoring and fault diagnosis applications
abstract: Firstly, the thesis addresses the problem caused by the limited availability of data for some classes (particularly fault classes), for supervised neural networks. Two novel techniques are developed to deal with this problem. The first of these techniques, referred to here as the 'Equal-Weightage' (EW) algorithm, involves a modification to the standard multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) training algorithm. The second approach, referred to here as 'Duplicate Data' (DD) training, is used to alter the configuration of the data set. Each technique is explored both theoretically and empirically, and is shown to result in significantly improved classifier performance.;Secondly, a 'fusion' classifier framework is developed which systematically addresses the issue of 'unclassified' and 'misclassified' patterns, in order to improve the performance of a classification system. The complete blackboard-based framework involves majority voting, Dempster-Shafer (D-S), MLP and expert system component. The D-S component involves a novel approach to mass assignment in D-S theory: an efficient implementation of this approach is also developed. Overall, the framework is seen to provide substantial improvements in classifier performance.;The techniques developed in the thesis are principally applied to the cooling system of a diesel engine. However, the techniques are also demonstrated in a different domain (classifying electrocardiographs) and it is argued that the results will prove valuable in a wider range of application areas in future studies.

title: Business plan for an innovative feminine medical device
abstract: The gynecological area related to vaginal infections is not very explored from the practical point of view of the patient. The range of options of self-testing kits is limited and little publicized, so women tend to go to the doctor whenever they feel any discomfort, or they simply buy medicine without a prescription. Therefore, a market opportunity arises to fill the lack of public information about this often neglected area of their personal health, without having to consult a doctor. This thesis explores the Femtech and Medtech market in Portugal and Europe. The business plan is about the launching of an innovative medical device to self-test vaginal infections and which connects to a mobile app to create records and analyticaly analyse the test results. This product’s aim is therefore to promote women’s well-being and health, allying with technology to inform them and subsequently help them to make decisions regarding their gynecological health.

title: Research on Maintenance Efficiency of Medical Equipment Based on Standardized Maintenance Texts
venue: International Journal of Medical Device Information
abstract: Objective This study focuses on medical equipment maintenance and explores the role of standardized maintenance texts in improving maintenance efficiency. Methods By analyzing the current status and existing deficiencies of hospital medical equipment maintenance, this paper adopts standardized maintenance texts to realize structured storage of maintenance data. The approach reduces ambiguous fault reporting and subjective descriptive deviation, while enhancing the quantitation, statistical performance and analytical value of maintenance data. Results Taking patient monitor fault maintenance as a typical case, the application of standardized maintenance texts significantly improved the rationality of maintenance resource allocation. The average response time of maintenance tasks was reduced by 20%, and the working efficiency of maintenance personnel increased by 15%. Conclusion Standardized maintenance texts can effectively shorten fault diagnosis time, optimize maintenance resource allocation, improve the availability of maintenance records, and provide solid data support for the full life cycle management of medical equipment. The findings provide a theoretical basis for the popularization and application of standardized maintenance texts in the medical equipment maintenance industry.

title: On AI-Based Maintenance of Medical Equipment in Home-Based Settings
abstract: The core aim of this proposition is to address the safety of vulnerable people as more and more healthcare is transferred from hospitals to homes. In that context medical equipment also needs to be brought into homes, and where such equipment itself needs to be monitored to ensure the safety of the care recipients. It has been shown that this is a critical issue, and the study of this contribution aims to approach such issues through modern AI-based techniques for predictive maintenance. This paper reflects on the first stage of a project in the context of healthcare taking place in homes, and where medical equipment needs digitized maintenance. Two preliminary experiments are presented, where those serve as prototypes and proof of concepts. On the one hand, ML-models to detect anomalies in data streams were developed and compared, and on the other hand, a radar system was developed where trilateration was used to locate movements of caretakers at home. Here, detecting falls were considered especially high priority, based on falls being common and serious accidents in homes. So far, experiments have shown promising results, and where an LSTM algorithm and an XGBoost algorithm are proposed for anomaly- and fall detections respectively.

title: Strategies for Optimizing the Management of Medical Equipment in Large Healthcare Institutions
venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Computer Science Engineering and Information Technology
abstract: Effective management of medical equipment is crucial in ensuring the operational efficiency, safety, and cost-effectiveness of healthcare institutions. As healthcare systems continue to evolve, the demand for advanced medical equipment and technologies grows, making the optimization of their management increasingly complex. This paper explores key strategies for optimizing medical equipment management in large healthcare institutions, focusing on overcoming operational inefficiencies, financial constraints, regulatory compliance, and technological integration barriers. Through adopting digital asset management systems, predictive maintenance, lifecycle cost analysis, and workforce training, healthcare institutions can significantly improve equipment utilization, reduce costs, and enhance patient care. The paper further examines industry case studies, benchmarking against standards, and emerging trends, such as using AI, blockchain, and cloud-based solutions in the healthcare sector. The findings highlight the importance of strategic policy implementation, investment in technology, and workforce development to address current challenges and prepare for future demands. Recommendations for healthcare providers and policymakers emphasize the need for data-driven decision-making, regulatory advancements, and sustainable procurement models to optimize medical equipment management. By integrating these strategies, healthcare institutions can achieve higher operational efficiency, improved patient outcomes, and enhanced regulatory compliance.

title: The Role of Sustainability and ESG in the Medical Device Sector
abstract: This chapter highlights the evolving landscape of medical device development under sustainability principles and emphasizes that the future of healthcare innovation will depend on the successful integration of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors without undermining clinical performance and safety. The medical device industry is undergoing a profound transformation as sustainability becomes an essential element of product development, manufacturing, and life cycle management. Regulatory pressures, growing environmental awareness, and the adoption of circular economy principles are driving manufacturers to rethink materials, design strategies, and operational practices. This shift is leading to the integration of biodegradable and recyclable materials, the refurbishment and modular design of high-cost equipment, and the implementation of take-back and recycling programs for electronic components and batteries. Furthermore, digitalization and artificial intelligence are contributing to sustainability through predictive maintenance, remote diagnostics, and the optimization of healthcare logistics. Despite clear progress, the sector faces significant challenges, including the high safety and performance standards required for medical devices, which can slow the introduction of eco-friendly innovations. Legal, regulatory, and economic barriers—especially for small and medium-sized enterprises—also complicate the widespread adoption of sustainable practices.
