title: Healthcare Depends on Quality Network Management
abstract: Sound network management practices are critical to most businesses, and even more so in healthcare. Keeping networked resources available at all times is the most fundamental aspect of network management, but, as we'll see, there's a lot going on behind the scenes to make it happen. Network downtime can cost a business financially in lost productivity and performance. For healthcare providers with medical information technology (IT) networks—defined as any IT network that incorporates at least one medical device—downtime can also impact patient care and safety.Network management is further stressed by constant growth and change. New applications will always be added, and old ones will be updated and upgraded. The networks themselves will change as new technology comes along to keep up with the ever increasing bandwidth demand. Networks are not bulletproof: Things will go wrong, resources will fail, and users will make mistakes.These are among the reasons for the new network risk management standard, IEC 80001-1. The standard, approved this fall, defines the roles, responsibilities, and activities that are necessary for risk management of medical IT networks to address safety, effectiveness, and data/system security. It focuses on risk management's means and processes for the entire life cycle of the medical IT network. We'll save the details of IEC 80001-1 for another IT World. In this issue, we'll focus on the other main tenets of what comprises network management. In addition, we'll look into the operation of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) as a model and a way to learn how this is accomplished.While recognizing that risk management is the overriding factor, there are five other key factors for a well-managed network: fault management, performance management, configuration management, accounting management, and security management. Before we get any further, it's important to mention the amount and effect of human intervention needed by the network manager. As we'll see, network management utilities are not fully automatic or autonomous.Fault management deals with quickly identifying, isolating, and repairing network problems. Many times, it's simply knowing who to reach out to when there's a problem. There are network technologies available that can notify the support staff when network components fail or network managers when server issues arise.Known as performance management, there are also applications that meter network operational parameters to help keep an eye on network health and predict imminent failure. Performance management involves tracking important network metrics such as processor and RAM usage, use of specific applications, disk access, and network traffic. Network status and performance information should be monitored continuously. Ideally, fault and performance monitoring should be proactive in detecting problems. This information can be used to forecast future upgrade requirements as well as troubleshoot network performance problems. However, it's only as proactive as the network manager's response.Tracking this kind of information can affect configuration management as well. Configuration management deals with adjusting network and user configurations to optimize network performance and productivity. Tied to fault management, changing configurations can additionally help to isolate network faults.Accounting management has to do with billing end-users for the applications and network resources they use. Internally, this means tracking use to ensure that you have enough licenses for the number of people using a particular application.One of the most important aspects of network management lies in security management. This means protecting the network from unauthorized internal or external access. You are susceptible to intrusion whenever you have an Internet connection point to your network.Authentication is the most common security measure used. This is simply user identification with a password and an access rights list of what can and cannot be accessed. If you are not given specific rights to a restricted resource, you will not be allowed access. There are also security authentication devices that generate activation codes. Some authentication devices require a personal identification number to gain network access. The device will then generate a random one-time password that allows log in. This process prevents a hacker from learning and using your password to log into the network disguised as you.In addition, there are techniques such as iris recognition. This biometric authentication method uses pattern-recognition techniques based on high-resolution images of an individual's eyes. Once confirmed, access is allowed.Part of security management is preventing viruses and other malware that can invade, deter, or destroy network function. Firewalls and firewall management become important tools for security management to help keep intruders out of your network.All of these aspects of network management are crucial to efficient and effective networks. Active management of the aspects can be a lot of work, especially as the network grows and evolves. However, there is constant development of new products and tools to assist in network management tasks. SNMP is one of the most important of these developments and really started the shift to formalized network management.One of the earliest and still most common of network management utilities is SNMP. It was designed to work within the TCP/IP network operating system. TCP/IP stands for Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol (IP). They were the first two networking protocols defined in the TCP/IP standard. Like many protocol suites, TCP/IP is constructed as a set of layers. Each layer solves a set of tasks involving network communication and the transmission of data. In particular, the layers define the operational scope of the protocols within. (See Figure 1.)SNMP established standards for collecting information and for performing the security, performance, fault, accounting, and configuration functions associated with network management. Examining SNMP is an excellent way to obtain an overall understanding of network management methods. Network management involves the use of various instruments to balance and optimize the network operation while keeping costs reasonable. SNMP provides the instruments and methods used for managing network device information. It accomplishes this with agents that run on each device to report back to managing systems.In 1988, SNMP version 1 (SNMPv1) was designed for the needs of the average IP implementer. IP networks are defined here as a collection of dissimilar networks joined together with bridges or routers. This initial implementation of the SNMP protocol became standardized in 1990. It operates over IP and the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). SNMPv1 is widely used and is the de facto network management protocol in the Internet community. It is the most common method by which network management applications can query a management agent using a supported management information base (MIB).There are three key components to SNMP:SNMP is typically configured to operate as either an NMS or an agent, but it can perform the functions of both. When a system operates as both, another NMS might require it to query its managed devices and provide a summary of the information learned. Another NMS might ask it to report its locally stored management information since it's also an agent.Managed devices are monitored and controlled with four basic SNMP commands:An MIB is a database of network performance data that is stored by a network agent for a NMS. It is comprised of managed objects (which are data or information pieces) and is uniquely identified by an object identifier (OID). An OID defines one of many specific characteristics of a managed device. OIDs are comprised of one or more “object instances,” which are the data, also called “variables.” For example, a managed object might contain a single object instance, such as an integer value that indicates the total number of input broadcast packets on a particular router interface. In addition, the MIB will know how to respond to standard queries issued by network management protocols.The SNMPv1 SMI (structure of management information) defines the MIB table structure to group the OIDs and their variables. Tables are indexed in rows in a way that allows SNMP to retrieve or alter a row with a Get, GetNext, or Set command.The MIB variables will contain statistics such as the number of packets dropped, packets sent, bytes sent, broadcast packets, multicast packets, CRC errors, runts, giants, fragments, jabbers, and collisions. The data might also list the numbers of packets by size in bytes. The MIB can record historical information such as: the sample period, number of samples, or what items were sampled. Alarms can also be tracked as they are derived from other data—NOT patient alarms; rather, network function alarms. The resultant alarm table portion of the MIB includes the alarm type, interval, and starting and stop thresholds. Information about the managed device will also be listed. This includes the host address and packet information in terms of who has it been communicating with. This is referred to as matrix information, and will have source and destination address pairs, and packets, bytes, and errors for each pair.SNMP commands are transmitted in a protocol data unit (PDU) format. Most SNMP PDUs are constructed as:The portions particular to SNMP PDU's are:There is also a trap PDU that has fields in it to send traps—or predefined status alerts—back to the NMS.The SNMP commands are further defined by specific message formats. There are seven types of messages that use the main PDU structure shown previously:Network management routines provide network administrators with comprehensive network-fault diagnosis, planning, and performance-tuning information. The use of this data is up to the network manager. It's also up to the network manager to configure alerts (set traps) to generally manage the network. The information provided allows the network manager to manage network configuration and to accumulate accounting and security related information. All of this information might contribute to an oversight risk assessment and management procedure as outlined in the IEC 80001-1 standard.In selecting a network management approach, the benefits must be weighed against costs, compatibility issues, and network requirements. SNMP is the most common method that provides for managing information about internetworked systems. An agent runs on each managed device and reports information to different NMSs. For example, if one of your servers is running out of disk space, you will want to know about it before it starts to affect your users.Information can be retrieved from an agent directly by requesting the information using a GET request. Information can also prompt the agent to send information to NMSs via a TRAP or INFORM message.In addition, NMSs can set information and parameters on the agent to change network configuration as needed. As listed in the earlier examples, the types of information that can be shared can be quite varied. It can be everything from basic network settings, statistics, and packet data for network interfaces to monitoring CPU load and disk space.This has been a high-level look at the basic network management components and methods. There is a lot more detail in SNMP not explored here: For example, SMI tables that list compliance and capability statements; the SMI table's MIB nodules that contain definitions of interrelated managed objects, and the detail outlining the difference between the three main versions of SNMP (SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and, especially, SMPv3). If interested, I recommend further investigation.Cisco has excellent information available at www.cisco.com: Search for the Internetworking Technology Handbook, where chapter 56 covers SNMP. There is also good information available from IBM: Go to www.ibm.com/developerworks/aix/library to utilize the technical library. While IBM covers a lot of technical information about its products, it can be useful to learn about how vendors approach and resolve particular network management issues that crop up. Happy hunting!

title: Foundations of artificial intelligence in healthcare IT: An overview of innovation
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is revolutionizing Healthcare IT by enhancing diagnostics, treatment planning, and patient monitoring. This overview explores key AI technologies, such as machine learning and natural language processing, driving innovation. AI enables data-driven decision-making, improving health outcomes, operational efficiency, and addressing challenges and ethical considerations in healthcare integration. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Healthcare IT, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, Patient Monitoring, Treatment Planning 1.1. Introduction to Hyperconverged Infrastructure (HCI) Artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to many fields, including healthcare. To improve healthcare deliverables, including diagnosis, treatment, and patient monitoring, subsets of AI, such as natural language processing, robotics, machine learning, and expert systems, have been deployed. Consequently, many papers have been produced that describe these applications. However, as healthcare decision-support tools, many recent AI applications deal with expensive, rare conditions and treatments that are not widely available for front-line healthcare professionals. This paper seeks to contribute to overcoming this bias by demonstrating utility in lower-prevalence settings (Syed, 2024). In recent years, the tremendous advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) research and applications is evident. Particularly, while taking advantage of enhancements in computing power, massive data sources, institutional investments, and myriad breakthroughs, rapid advances, including applications on multiple task forms, have been witnessed in machine learning (ML) and deep learning. Concurrently, many new AI techniques and related applications have emerged. Specifically, significant benefits have been achieved via AI tools and methods, particularly where high-throughput, highly complex tasks are involved. However intriguing these tremendous advances have been, the researchers who seek to develop and deploy AI methodologies face a unique set of challenges in the domain of healthcare. 1.1.1. Background and Significance Embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is not just the talk of imminent frontiers of technology-driven innovation, but is a very current affair. Business plans, resources, and disciplines are lining up to provide new IT infrastructures for developing innovative healthcare systems. In the IT industry, innovation is considered a catalyst for business growth and profitability. Business leaders seek to drive innovation in products, reduce costs, and tie new technology systems more directly to the business community(Ramanakar, 2024). IT departments, and innovators themselves, emerge as potential enablers, demonstrating their ability to create value from new and disruptive technologies. Cloud, analytics, mobile, and AI technologies come together today to achieve healthcare-related business goals, providing better healthcare for greater audiences in need. Drastically reducing the time and cost of drug synthesis, as well as providing precision medicine to a targeted set of patients, will be a direct consequence of AI models applied to drug target identification, clinical trial design and execution, patient history, and other multidimensional patient data processing. The recent spike in interest for such tasks has been driven by the rise of very large and complex datasets, machine learning, and other related technologies improvement, readily available cloud computing infrastructure, and an influx of new IT specialists specialized in data protection and healthcare. Numerous commercially successful AI startups are currently driving value by embedding AI into existing information technology infrastructures; in areas such as electronic health record improvement, reimbursement and claims management, clinical trial management, personalized medicine offerings, and telemedicine support tools. Fig 1 . 1 : Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Research. 1.1.2. Research Aim and Objectives By addressing this research aim, related sub-aims were identified. Firstly, the concept and dimensions of artificial intelligence and healthcare IT were considered and reviewed. AI concepts and transformation were synthesized within the confines of healthcare IT. To achieve this aim, the objectives were also established. Although AI has been gaining attention in recent years, it is still immature in healthcare practice. The prominent deficiency of artificial intelligence is due to the applied up-to-date methodology. The goals of this research will lead to preliminary studies on how much AI is used in the healthcare sector, and the results will produce a model for decision-makers to use AI systems, resulting in increased patient-healthcare provider satisfaction and improved healthcare quality. The framework will provide a reference for AI developers and mitigate AI's prominent deficiencies. The successful utilization model alignment can produce a model for integrating AI into future healthcare systems, promoting popularity and usability (Nampalli, 2024). 1.2. Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Over the past few years, the domain of professional tasks carried out in healthcare settings that utilize technology-based components of computer-like systems, referred to as healthcare information technology, has expanded considerably. The data generated in electronic health records, called clinical data, are a valuable resource for research, health professionals, and patients themselves, but we are still in an exploratory stage regarding their use. One of the promising uses of clinical data involves providing the user with knowledge about a field such as clinical reasoning, for example, recurrently directing a rational choice. For this reason, the methodology and techniques of the discipline that deals with the use of computing to formally reason, called artificial intelligence, are being expressly applied in healthcare settings. The set of tools and techniques used to conceive computer-like systems, as they relate to tasks that, when done by humans, are often said to require intelligence, brings together several fields of knowledge under the name of artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence is the science and engineering of making intelligent machines—a technology capable of creating an entirely new world that satisfies human beings, the best development of nature. Artificial intelligence is a highly interdisciplinary field situated at the intersection of computer science, physics, mathematics, psychology, and economics. The basic goal of artificial intelligence is to create programs that perform tasks, many of which can only be handled effectively by a human due to being solved by human reasoning, knowledge, and experience, such as diagnosis, advice, planning, and learning. Artificial intelligence, as performed in the academic or corporate setting, deals with intelligent behavior, i.e., solving tasks that human experts would carry out. To achieve the goal of creating programs that exhibit the same behavior as humans do, researchers often use a metaphor called symbolic learning and algorithms that generalize decision rules from empirical examples to find the rules. These rules are intended to mimic human expert knowledge and use them to solve new problems. 1.2.1. Definition and Scope AI is the part of computer science that attempts to emulate human intelligence or act intelligently (reason, perceive, communicate, and so forth) as a human. It is a multidisciplinary area and aims not only at discovering the principles that govern our intelligence and consciousness but also at bringing them into reality in a variety of artificial systems. AI research has a long history, dating back to ancient times. At present, there are many problems to address in the field, and a variety of approaches to understanding and building are being proposed (Maguluri et al., 2024). Though general intelligence remains science fiction, the best AI systems are quite sophisticated and capable of great achievements. In medicine, AI comprises a variety of technologies: intelligence and learning are essential qualities, but knowledge and expertise are also necessary elements. These qualities have been built by human specialists into many systems that automate, extend, and support everyday medical activities. The use of these AI systems is not technically new; the earliest ones were already being used by medical researchers, practitioners, and administrators in the early 1970s. AI systems and AI technology have continued to evolve, adding new capabilities and demonstrating increased performance throughout the years. These systems already provide direct benefits for practicing clinicians, research scientists, and healthcare organizations. Indeed, the stage is now set for an explosion of opportunity and innovation as the cards of technology, data quality, and recognition of clinical needs are combined with enhanced vision, clinician input, and policy implementation. Applications in Healthcare IT Biomedical informatics and the enabling technology of healthcare information technology (IT) have historically focused on improving the delivery of healthcare or therapy to a patient. The term “biomedical informatics” denotes the discipline or field of research, and “healthcare information technology” refers to the mechanics of applying technology for capturing, processing, and electronically transmitting data relevant to patient care or conducting clinical research inquiries. In healthcare, we broadly consider the delivery of patient care to encompass not only therapeutic and preventive care but also the diagnosis of disease, monitoring of patient condition, and many pedagogical or administrative aspects of patient care. The diagnostic and monitoring functions both connect with the physiology of the patient and support physician requirements for valid medical findings, healthcare IT also needs to connect with the healthcare provider processes that contribute information to the diagnostic or monitoring interpretation (Ravi et al., 2022). Diagnostic and Monitoring Devices The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a classic example of a clinical monitoring measurement that has advanced greatly in part due to informatics-driven changes in measurement modality. It is traditionally a fairly complex and invasive point measurement made intermittently under controlled inpatient settings, soon followed by some form of manual reading, possibly resulting in immediate and life-saving therapy. With portable and semi-invasive multipoint or continuous monitoring, however, we see the capture of much more clinically relevant information and the potential for better and earlier diagnoses and outpatient management. Providing experienced interpretation continually also becomes an issue, as does the storage and management of information from a potentially large patient pool. This dynamic is common to other vital signs, imaging data, and even the patient’s subjective symptomology. 1.3. Innovations in AI for Healthcare Because of the size of AI as an area of research, I do not aim to give an exhaustive list that includes all ideas and trends in the field. I intend to provide readers with a general overview of important and meaningful innovation in healthcare. Readers new to the field can use the examples in the paper to identify their area of interest. There is a wide range of techniques that are classified as AI or algorithmic innovations. Some of the oldest and most widely used AI methods are rule-based systems that can capture expert knowledge in the form of condition-action rules. Classical rule-based systems work well for problems that can be described or encoded by a set of rules. Moreover, rule-based systems are easy to understand and much easier to debug. They are especially useful when human judgment is involved. Neural network processing units are modeled on the biological nervous system. The NN consists of layers of artificial neurons connected in a network. The deeper the network, the greater its complexity. Deep or hierarchical artificial neural networks also provide different layers of processing units. These layers, from lower to higher levels of abstraction, are used for the detection of features or patterns of input data, which process the output data. One of the commonly used techniques is decision trees, which are nonetheless simple—often they are the basic idea used by an expert. Input data is used to progressively reduce the uncertainty of an outcome based upon some specific algorithmic rules, which are learned from example data. Additionally, the practical flexibility provided by decision tree models generally comes equipped with zero extra costs, which makes them highly useful model families that are capable of performing tens of thousands of predictions for patients each year (Tulasi et al., 2022). When dealing with tabular data, ensemble methods, though not an algorithmic innovation, have greatly advanced by allowing us more flexible integration of features into larger predictive models via the application of multiple simple models. Similarly, boosting is the idea of combining models to improve predictive strength. 1.3.1. Machine Learning Algorithms Three types of machine learning algorithms are widely used and developed: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. From past experiences or training by the domain expert, supervised learning algorithms learn the input and output pairs and make predictions on new data. Supervised learning has two subcategories: regression and classification. Regression is used to predict the continuous output, and regression analysis tries to explain the relationship between input and output as certain mathematical functions. In contrast, classification is often used for discrete output and is a problem when the algorithm needs to approximate a function that maps a continuous feature into a category head. Widely used classification algorithms include Random Forest, deep learning, decision tree, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, inductive logic programming, and Naive Bayes. Deep learning is a type of machine learning algorithm with multiple levels of learning and can be applied to many robotic tasks, such as image, video, and speech recognition, which are all useful for healthcare applications. Used for clustering patients in different situations, unsupervised learning does not have any prior training data from the domain but can successfully conduct the learning and make a model with the clusters of input data. Common tasks in healthcare with unsupervised algorithms include patient clustering, patient sub-typing, anomaly detection, and topic modeling. title: Editorial: Generative AI and large language models in medicine: applications, challenges, and opportunities
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has entered medicine through a heterogeneous set of uses rather than through a single technological pathway. Large language models now draft clinical text, interpret reports, answer patient questions, support knowledge retrieval, structure health data, assist education, and participate in increasingly complex decision support workflows. The 34 contributions assembled in this Research Topic capture that breadth across clinical medicine, public health, digital health, oncology, rehabilitation, mental health, nursing, health informatics, education, quality management, and biomedical policy. Their collective value lies less in any single performance estimate than in the opportunity to examine what changes when language model research moves from demonstrations of linguistic competence toward systems that must operate under clinical constraints.The studies concerned with diagnosis, staging, and clinical reasoning show why this distinction matters. In a two institution study of 552 PET CT reports across six cancers, Xu et al. found that GPT 5 achieved 82.1 percent overall TNM staging accuracy compared with 77.0 percent for junior radiologists, while repeated model agreement was close to perfect. Performance nevertheless differed across cancer types and was weakest for metastatic staging. Dinç et al. reported an analogous pattern in radiation oncology. GPT 5 reached 92.8 percent on a standardized examination benchmark, substantially exceeding earlier GPT generations, yet authentic clinical vignettes still produced substantive errors in cases requiring precise trial knowledge or detailed adaptation to clinical context. The high benchmark score therefore did not remove the need for specialist review.Other studies reinforce the task dependent character of performance. Pan et al. found that DeepSeek V3.1, ChatGPT 5, and Grok 4 answered more than 90 percent of guideline derived bone cancer questions correctly in both evaluation rounds, although model specific strengths remained. In maternal venous thromboembolism care, Li et al. found superior overall expert ratings for GPT 4.1, Claude 3.7, and DeepSeek across education, care planning, and prevention, but explicitly did not interpret those results as evidence of readiness for independent nursing deployment. Konzmann et al., synthesizing 31 tumor board studies and 3,845 cases, identified a broader complexity gap: concordance was strongest in standardized and common oncological settings and deteriorated in rare, multimodal, or clinically ambiguous cases.This evidence is compatible with the conceptual position advanced by Greengrass, who treats AI as a potential support for human clinical reasoning rather than as a replacement for it. Human reasoning is constrained by working memory, cognitive load, fatigue, anchoring, and other biases, whereas computational systems can search and compare information at scales that exceed unaided cognition. The collection, however, does not support the inference that computational scale removes clinical uncertainty. Its more defensible implication is a risk gradient. Language models appear most reliable when the task has explicit rules, sufficiently complete textual evidence, and an auditable reference standard. Their reliability becomes more difficult to establish as the task requires multimodal interpretation, rare disease knowledge, rapidly changing evidence, patient specific tradeoffs, or judgments for which several clinically defensible answers may exist.A second theme concerns the architecture surrounding the language model. Several contributions suggest that the clinically relevant object is increasingly the full system rather than the foundation model in isolation. Barlow et al. fine-tuned an open Llama model to identify actionable incidental findings in PET CT reports and achieved a document level F1 score of 0.917 internally and 0.79 on an external test set. The reduction under external evaluation is itself informative, because differences in reporting style and institutional practice remain consequential even when internal performance is strong.Grounding methods address a different source of error. Kokash et al. combined ontology-based retrieval with LLM semantic adjudication for healthcare data harmonization and reported expert agreement as high as 92 percent. Retrieval alone was insufficient; the gain came from pairing broad candidate retrieval with model based semantic validation. Chen et al. provide a related demonstration through a knowledge graph system for Jin San Zhen therapy. Their hybrid architecture outperformed the general model on correctness, professionalism, and completeness, while the knowledge enhanced outputs remained traceable to source literature and no fabricated claims were detected in the evaluated question set. Sugihara et al. extend this architectural reasoning to the choice between open and proprietary models. Proprietary systems may offer stronger schema adherence or complex reasoning in some tasks, whereas open models provide advantages in local control, auditability, customization, privacy, and cost. The practical choice therefore depends on the clinical task and governance environment rather than on a universal model ranking.Bounded documentation and evidence processing tasks may be among the more defensible near term applications, but they still require verification. Aiumtrakul et al. found strong clinical reasoning in 89.7 percent of ChatGPT 5 generated nephrology prior authorization letters, yet diagnostic coding was correct in 79.3 percent and citation errors remained. Oami et al. observed high performance for background data extraction in systematic reviews, but outcome extraction was markedly more variable and repeated session consistency declined for the harder task. More elaborate prompting produced only modest accuracy changes while increasing processing time. Khoruzhaya et al. place these findings in methodological context: their review of medical text summarization reported external validation in only 7 percent of studies and patient safety assessment in only 3 percent, with wide variation in reported hallucination rates. Their MEDAI LLM SUMM checklist accordingly emphasizes clinical validity, prompt documentation, expert evaluation, hallucination assessment, safety, and data availability. Zhu et al., using eight models to generate medical examination questions and answers from real world EHRs, further show that models can approach clinicians on selected dimensions while human authors retain advantages in information sufficiency and overall answer quality.Taken together, these studies distinguish prompt engineering from clinical system engineering. Prompt design can improve instructions, but evidence grounding, model adaptation, structured outputs, local deployment, source traceability, safety rules, and expert adjudication determine whether an apparently competent model can be integrated into a reproducible workflow.Patient facing applications expose another limitation of accuracy centered evaluation. Graca et al. found that healthcare professionals rated ChatGPT responses more favourably than established evidence based PCOS responses for 11 of 12 questions, and further simplification improved readability. Yet the wider collection shows that medical correctness does not guarantee communicative usefulness. Joseph et al. found that cardiovascular responses changed in complexity with the education level implied by the prompt, but output frequently remained above ordinary health literacy needs. Wang et al. on gestational diabetes reported 92.17 percent mean accuracy for ChatGPT 5 on standardized questions and favourable reliability ratings, while all evaluated models still exceeded the recommended sixth grade reading level and showed poor transparency under JAMA criteria. Huang et al. reached a similar result for perinatal depression: responses were often informative and empathetic, but readability remained excessive and clinical safety behaviours were incomplete.The chronic heart failure study by Wang et al. on chronic heart failure adds actionability to this evaluation framework. Overall content quality was favourable, but median actionability was only 20 percent, and the most complete output was also among the least readable. This reveals a structural tradeoff that cannot be captured by accuracy alone. Albaz et al. likewise found favourable clarity and tone in ChatGPT 5 responses about vasectomy, but medical accuracy and completeness varied across questions and expert agreement was very low. Patient validation was absent. Angyal et al. approach the same problem from the user side by developing a questionnaire to measure how adults use ChatGPT for primary and secondary disease prevention, providing a basis for studying behaviour rather than assuming that availability translates into appropriate use.Two contributions show how patient and caregiver support may be made more constrained. Hanzawa et al. combined a domain specific knowledge base, retrieval augmented generation, sentiment analysis, explicit safety restrictions, and escalation rules in an agent supporting families implementing treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa. Experts rated 91.6 percent of 477 responses as clinically appropriate, but the authors appropriately call for usability testing and randomized evaluation of caregiver burden, adherence, and clinical outcomes. O'Malley et al. similarly describe retrieval, system instructions, and fine tuning as complementary strategies for customized physical activity chatbots, while emphasizing human evaluation, privacy, and operational cost.These studies support a multidimensional definition of patient facing quality. Accuracy and completeness remain necessary, but safe communication also requires readability, actionability, source traceability, uncertainty communication, cultural and educational fit, and evidence that users understand what the system has told them.Clinical implementation depends on professionals as well as models. Among Italian physiotherapists, Deodato et al. found widespread awareness of AI chatbots but limited clinical use: 66.9 percent had never used them in practice even though 78 percent expressed a positive attitude toward future adoption. Concerns centred on patient self diagnosis, false information, and loss of human interaction. In a sample drawn principally from Ecuador, Cherrez Ojeda et al. similarly found cautious optimism, but only 31.99 percent had used ChatGPT and 67.85 percent of familiar respondents regarded sole source clinical use as unethical. Safi et al. documented a different mismatch in surgical education: 80.9 percent had prior ChatGPT experience, yet 93.2 percent lacked formal AI training. Informal exposure is therefore advancing faster than structured professional education.The multimodal papers widen the definition of clinical AI while also illustrating why adding data modalities should not be assumed to improve performance. Manir et al. combined textual embeddings with acoustic summaries for affective tone analysis in aphasia. Under recording separated evaluation, the fused model did not outperform the text only model, and human agreement on aphasic affect was low. Hussain et al. review evidence in depression detection showing benefits from combining EEG, speech, facial, and linguistic signals, but also report the familiar decline from controlled laboratory results to more ecologically representative datasets. Siefert et al. demonstrate that smaller fine tuned models can approximate expert psychological ratings of complex narratives, particularly when model outputs are ensembled, yet they retain human supervision as the appropriate clinical frame.Multimodality also creates new risks. Jędrasiak and Bijoch examine synthetic audiovisual material in telemedicine and teledentistry, showing that manipulation can threaten diagnostic evidence, communication, and medico legal documentation. Their work makes provenance part of clinical safety. Trustworthy generative AI cannot be defined only by whether generated text is factually correct; healthcare systems must also be able to establish whether the data supplied to an AI system, or returned through a digital encounter, are authentic.The collection therefore shifts attention from model capability toward an evaluation and governance problem. Knott et al. show that healthcare AI studies still concentrate disproportionately on accuracy while paying far less attention to fairness, calibration, deployment readiness, and actual patient care. Their European analysis also makes clear that regulatory obligations depend on intended function and clinical risk. Administrative quality tools and systems that influence diagnosis or treatment cannot be governed as equivalent applications. Wang, Hao and Chen extend the accountability question into pharmaceutical intellectual property, where AI assisted discovery raises unresolved issues concerning inventorship, copyright, and ownership across jurisdictions.Reproducibility deserves particular attention. A clinical system that changes a medically material recommendation when the patient information has not changed poses a different problem from a deterministic medical device, even if its average performance is favourable. The tumor board literature synthesized by Konzmann et al. reports substantial variation in repeated response consistency and incomplete reporting of model inference settings across studies. Oami et al. likewise show that repeated session consistency can deteriorate as extraction becomes more complex. Model updates introduce another layer of temporal instability because the product evaluated today may not be behaviourally identical to the product deployed later.The evidence across the Research Topic supports a risk proportionate interpretation of human oversight. Lower consequence, reversible, and auditable tasks such as drafting, extraction, summarization, and guideline retrieval are plausible candidates for supervised implementation. Patient communication and guideline based decision support require stronger controls because deficiencies in readability, actionability, or omitted context may affect behaviour. Diagnosis, staging, treatment recommendation, and other high consequence applications require prospective validation, explicit uncertainty handling, and clinician accountability. Human review should therefore be designed into the workflow rather than appended as a generic disclaimer.Figure 1 represents this translational logic. Foundation model capability is only the first stage. Task adaptation must be followed by evidence grounding, workflow integration, clinical validation, and continuous governance. Human oversight, external validation, reproducibility, evidence traceability, health literacy and equity, privacy, and accountability operate across the pathway rather than at a single endpoint. This structure also explains why no universally superior medical language model emerges from the collection. Different systems lead on different endpoints, and the preferred model changes with the task, population, infrastructure, privacy requirements, and tolerance for error. The 34 contributions document a field moving from proof of language competence toward the science of accountable clinical integration. Contemporary models can perform useful work in structured clinical reasoning, data extraction, patient education, documentation, knowledge retrieval, psychological assessment, and administrative processes. They can sometimes match or exceed junior clinicians or established information sources on narrowly defined measures. Those findings are scientifically relevant, but they are not equivalent to evidence of autonomous clinical readiness.The next phase of research should therefore privilege prospective and multicentre evaluation, external validation across institutions and populations, repeated testing for response stability, explicit reporting of model versions and inference conditions, patient centred endpoints, economic evaluation, fairness assessment, and post deployment surveillance. Grounded architectures using curated retrieval, ontologies, knowledge graphs, local models, and explicit escalation rules warrant continued evaluation because they make model behaviour more constrained and auditable. Clinical AI literacy must develop in parallel so that professionals can judge uncertainty, verify sources, protect patient data, recognize inappropriate automation, and retain responsibility for consequential decisions.Generative AI is becoming useful in medicine before it has become uniformly trustworthy. The evidence in this Research Topic suggests that the appropriate response is neither unrestricted adoption nor categorical rejection. The defensible path is selective integration in which technical capability is matched to clinical risk, evidence is made traceable, validation extends beyond benchmark accuracy, and accountability remains explicit throughout the system lifecycle.

Gen: Alert and oriented, in no apparent distress. HEENT: normal. Heart: normal with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs: Clear bilaterally with decreased air entry and pain with inspiration. No retractions, no tracheal tugging. Extremities: Bilateral swelling of the legs with tenderness to palpation of the right calf. No induration, no erythema, no ecchymosis. CTA chest: Bilateral pulmonary emboli with no large central embolus FINAL WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Unprovoked DVT with pulmonary emboli TREATMENT AND OUTCOMES: Pt was treated with anticoagulants at an outside facility and held out of sport for 6 months. (No relationships reported) HISTORY: A 21 year old NCAA Div 1 football linebacker suffered blunt abdominal trauma as he fell onto the quarterback’s foot while making the tackle. Play was stopped for on-field evaluation, and he complained of “getting the wind knocked out of him.” He was able to ambulate to the sideline. At this time his abdominal pain improved slightly, but not as much as expected from his prior self diagnosis. We then held him from the game. Though he remained ambulatory, his pain plateau’d and serial exams were concerning for internal injury. He was transported to the emergency department for further evaluation. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: VS BP 130-138/80-90 P 60-68 (serial rechecks). In no distress. Cardiac and pulmonary exams were normal. Abdomen soft, nondistended, but mild epigastric, RUQ, and suprapubic pain to palpation. CVA palpation caused anterior RUQ pain. No rebound or guarding. Serial exams neither improved nor worsened. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: 1. Abdominal/rib contusion 2. Renal contusion/laceration 3. Liver contusion/laceration 4. Pancreatic contusion/laceration 5. Hollow organ injury 6. Ureteral rupture/transection TEST AND RESULTS: Imaging: Contrast CT:liver laceration with no continued extravasation and small hemoperitoneum. Repeat contrast CT:stable liver laceration with concern for post traumatic arterio-venous fistula. Ultrasound: negative. Angiography: arterio-venous fistula and performed gel embolization. Third contrast CT:stable liver laceration but continued concern for small fistula. Labwork: Hgb=12.1-12.8 ALT=270 (H) trended down to 136 (H) AST=272 (H) trended down to 45 (H) Final working diagnosis: Grade 3 liver laceration and post traumatic arterio-venous fistula. TREATMENT AND OUTCOMES: Patient monitored in the trauma ICU uneventfully. Grade 3 liver laceration achieved hemostasis on its own; no surgical treatment was necessary. Interventional radiology embolized the arterio-venous fistula. As the liver laceration was stable, on day 6 he was discharged home. The persistent AV fistula was small, and both IR and liver surgery felt it best to be managed conservatively. Repeat contrast CT at 4 weeks planned. The fistula may require another procedure at that time. He is prohibited from moderate to strenuous activities in the meanwhile. Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, WI. He originally was found to have thrombocytopenia in January 2012, after a CBC revealed his platelet count to be 75,000. He is a transfer student who did not receive the recommended repeat lab testing at his previous college. He denies any bleeding complications (epistaxis, hematuria, melena, hematochezia, easy bruising). He has no other chronic medical conditions. He currently takes finasteride (1 mg) daily for male-pattern baldness. Sexually active, always uses barrier contraception. Drinks 5-10 beers on the weekends, none during the week. Denies illicit drug use. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: -Vitals: Ht 5’10”, Wt 179 lbs, BMI 25.43, T 98.1 F, BP 134/73, P 72, R 16 -Gen: Well-appearing, no acute distress -ENT: oropharynx clear, moist mucous membranes, anicteric -CV: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs -Resp: Clear to auscultation bilaterally -Abd: Soft, nontender, nondistended. No hepatosplenomegaly. -Skin: No rashes, jaundice, or petechiae PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: -Pseudothrombocytopenia -Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) -Drug-induced thrombocytopenia -Myelodysplasia TEST AND RESULTS: -CBC: WBC 3.8 (L), Hgb 15.7, Hematocrit 44, Platelets 85 (L) -Mean platelet volume: 12.9 (H) -Peripheral smear: moderate thrombocytopenia with giant platelets; otherwise normal RBC/WBC morphology FINAL WORKING DIAGNOSIS: -Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) TREATMENT AND OUTCOMES: 1. There is little guidance in literature about a threshold for platelets to allow safe participation in contact/collision sports. 2. Hematologist suggested monitoring platelet counts monthly and allowing football participation if platelet count stays above 50,000, provided he does not have associated splenomegaly. 3. 50,000 was used as threshold since elective surgeries are typically delayed if platelet counts are <50,000. 4. Instructed patient to stop all alcohol consumption as well as finasteride, which have the potential to cause thrombocytopenia. 5. Abdominal ultrasound performed, showed no evidence of splenomegaly. 6. Patient continues to play this season, last platelet count was 68,000. No issues with participation. 3039 June 1, 10:00 AM - 10:20 AM Skin Rash in a Walker Dan Cushman, Monica Rho. Rehabilitation Institute of Chicago, Chicago, IL. (No relationships reported) HISTORY: A 40-year-old gentleman presented to our outpatient sports & spine center with the complaint of progressive bilateral medial calcaneal pain that was worse in the morning and better with walking. He had increased his walking significantly over the past month from being sedentary to walking a few miles per day. He had no other focal musculoskeletal, vascular, or neurologic complaints. He also noticed a new non-pruritic, non-painful “rash” on both of his ankles and feet which appeared insidiously over that time. He used primarily Birkenstock sandals or short socks with “Skechers” shoes (both of which were not brought to the office for inspection) while walking, and walked outdoors. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Exam revealed inferomedial calcaneal tenderness bilaterally. There were no other focal neurologic or musculoskeletal findings with the exception of tight calf musculature bilaterally. Skin exam revealed bilateral nontender, nonblanchable, scattered light-brown macules on bilateral medial malleoli and dorsum of the distal foot, sparing the midfoot. See Figure. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Exercise-induced vasculitis Contact dermatitis Cellulitis Venous insufficiency Drug eruption Systemic vasculitis TEST AND RESULTS: No diagnostic tests were performed. FINAL WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Exercise-induced vasculitis TREATMENT AND OUTCOMES: The patient was offered topical steroids for his dermatitis, but as he was asymptomatic and understood that his condition is generally a self-limited process, he chose watchful waiting. He was unable to be reached for follow-up after his diagnosis was made. 3040 June 1, 10:20 AM - 10:40 AM Fever- Male Soccer Brian Cruickshank, Jeanne Doperak. UPMC St. Margaret, Pittsburgh, PA. (No relationships reported) HX: 21yo M div 1 collegiate soccer player in mod distress presents to the training room. Reports 4 days of general fatigue with chills, rigors, myalgias, and nausea. Now with frequent, watery, non-bloody stools. Recently returned from Nigeria after attending a funeral. Because of the sudden unexpected travel, there had been no pre-travel medications or vaccinations. Brother, who was also traveling with family, just diagnosed with malaria PE: Denies CP, SOB, abd pain but does c/o gen abd cramping. 39.4, 94, 115/68, 18, 99%. Well developed male, mod distress, appears fatigued. NCAT, PERRL, moist oral mucosa. Neck supple, no cervical lymph. Heart regular. Abd soft, NTND, no rebound tenderness/guarding, hyperactive bowel sounds. No bony/soft tissue abnormalities. Alert, answering questions appropriately, no focal deficits. No apparent rashes/lesions/insect bites DIFFERENTIAL: 1 Gastroenteritis 2 Travelers Diarrhea 3 Appendicitis 4 Influenza 5 Malaria 6 Dengue 7 Typhoid 8 Yellow Fever 9 Abdominal Abscess TESTS/RESULTS: CXR: Clear lungs, normal heart size ECG: NSR Urine/stool cx: UA- neg, U cx- stenotrophomonas maltophilia. Stool cx- neg salmonella/shigella/campylobacter/E coli. Stool ova/parasites- absent. C diff toxin/Crypto smear- neg. Stool WBCs- present. Giardia Ag- not detected Blood work: BMP/LFTs- normal. CBC with diff- platelets 110 and dohle bodies present in WBCs. LDH- 252. Haptoglobin- 64.6. CPK- 321. Blood cultures- (+)SALMONELLA species. Anti HAV Ab total/IgM,Hep E IgG/IgM, Lyme IgG/IgM, West nile virus smear, HIV- neg. Dengue Fever Ab IgG/IgM- <.90. Abd US: mild splenomegaly FINAL WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Typhoid/parathyphoid fever TREATMENT/OUTCOMES: Admitted for fever in setting of recent travel. Initially aggressive rehydration, anti-pyretics and anti-inflammatories. Started on Ceftriaxone 1gm IV q24hrs for presumed Travelers diarrhea but increased to 2gm IV q24hrs after blood cultures with gram neg rods in 4/4 aerobic and anaerobic bottles. After 4 days inpatient treatment, repeat blood cultures were neg for 48hrs. Pt was transitioned to Ciprofloxicin 500mg po bid and DC home. Given his sport and mild splenomegaly was advised not to participate until repeat abd US 1 week. Repeat US showed regression of splenomegaly. Athlete released from team after being unable to participate in preseason 3041 June 1, 10:40 AM - 11:00 AM Safe To Scuba? David S. Edwards. Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center, School of Medicine, Lubbock, TX. (No relationships reported) HISTORY: A 64 year old male presented for physical exam to determine medical fitness for SCUBA diving. His past medical history was significant for diabetes mellitus type II, hypertension, obesity, and intermittent low back pain. He did desk-based work but walked 1 mile on a treadmill three times a week. Blood glucoses were typically in the 120-150 mg/dl range. His goal was to dive to a depth of 80 feet for 30 minutes without rapid ascent. He reported compliance with his medications which were: metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and naproxen 220 mg every 8 hours as needed. He denied previous hospitalizations. He did not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. On review of systems, he denied: seizures or history of stroke, headaches, chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea on exertion, dizziness with exercise, syncope, wheezing, and hypoglycemic episodes. He lost 20 pounds intentionally over the past year. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Temp. 98.2°, BP 122/82, HR 60, RR 12, BMI 30. Pertinent findings on exam were: absence of carotid bruits, auscultation of clear lungs, regular heart rate and rhythm without murmur or gallop, soft abdomen, non-tender lumbar spine with intact range of motion and negative straight leg raise, 2+ pedal and carotid pulses, and non-focal neurologic exam. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: 1. Occult coronary artery disease 2. Occult peripheral vascular disease TEST AND RESULTS: Unremarkable CBC and CMP, Hemoglobin A1C 6.4, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 21, urine microalbumin < 1.2, Cholesterol 189, LDLc 117, HDLc 28, triglycerides 220, Apo B 94, 9P21 genotype heterozygous. EKG showed normal sinus rhythm, left axis deviation, and Q waves in leads III and aVF. Ultrasound CIMT of the common carotid arteries showed a total plaque burden of 3.4 mm. A thallium stress test showed an inferior, reversible defect. Coronary angiogram showed no hemodynamically significant occlusions and an ejection fraction of 65%. FINAL WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Diabetes mellitus II controlled, Dyslipidemia, Non-occlusive coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, vitamin D deficiency TREATMENT AND OUTCOMES: -placed on statin therapy -supplemented vitamin D -cleared to participate in scuba diving classes upon completion of an online diabetes mellitus educational program through the Divers Alert Network

The ultra-miniature sensor is manufactured directly at the tip of a 125-µm optical fiber, providing an all-glass device assembled without the use of any adhesive. It is biocompatible and suitable for integration in medical devices and in minimally invasive instrument catheters. The front-facing FOP-F125 allows in situ measurements at locations unreachable by standard pressure sensors. The sensor’s high resolution and precision in its pressure range of ±300 mmHg, combined with a fast reading rate, are important when users attempt to detect very quick and subtle pressure variations. The optical nature of the FOP-F125 makes the sensor immune to electromagnetic field or RF interference regularly encountered in operating rooms or MRI devices.
